newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU forecasts German deficit above EMU target - paper.
newsitem.headline: EU forecasts German deficit above EMU target - paper.

text.p: The European Commission forecasts that Germany's 1997 budget deficit will be above the target for a single European currency, a Portuguese newspaper reported on Thursday.

According to the report, published in El Publico, the European Union executive puts Germany's budget deficit this year at 3.2 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), just above the three percent target set in the Maastricht treaty to qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU).
A representative from the newspaper told Reuters that the figures had been obtained from the Commission.
But the report, which also put Italy's 1997 deficit at 3.8 percent of total output, was played down by Commission officials, who said the actual forecasts would not be ready until April 23.
"We have nothing to do with the table. Work on the forecast is still continuing," a Commission spokesman said.
When asked whether the information was wrong, the spokesman said: "We never make any comment on this sort of press speculation."

The report indicated that France and Spain were forecast to meet the Maastricht target. Overall, 12 out 15 countries were at or below the three percent deficit target, with only Germany, Greece and Italy not qualifying.
In the past, the Commission has been known to revise its economic estimates just days before an official release date, raising the possiblity that further revisions might be made.

But speculation that Bonn would have a tough time adhering strictly to the deficit target has been rampant in recent weeks, with sluggish economic growth and high unemployment contributing to an increasingly uncertain budget outlook.

Quoted in a magazine article on Thursday, Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen said: "It is becoming increasingly evident that Germany will find it extraordinarily difficult to meet the budget and debt criteria."
He also said a delay to the planned January 1, 1999 start date for monetary union could not be ruled out.

In contrast, Finance Minister Theo Waigel said recent economic data would not force Bonn to abandon its budget forecasts. But should there be a need for additional measures, Germany would be ready to act.
His views were echoed by Chancellor Helmut Kohl, who together with French President Jacques Chirac reaffirmed their expectations for a timely launch of the common currency.
An Italian Treasury source said Italy's recently introduced mini-budget would bring this year's deficit down to 3.0 percent of GDP.
The source added that the reported 3.8 percent figure referred to state accounts before the mini-budget was presented.

While meeting the deficit target has attracted the most attention among the numerous criteria countries must fulfil in order to join EMU, officials say it will also be important to assess whether budget consolidation is sustainable.
EU Monetary Commissioner Yves Thibault de Silguy recently said such an assessment would include a look at 1998 budget estimates.
Following are the deficit estimates by the Commission due on April 23, according to the Portuguese paper:
Spring 1997 (percent of GDP)
Belgium 2.8
Denmark 0.3
Germany 3.2
Greece 4.9
Spain 3.0
France 3.0
Ireland 0.8
Italy 3.8
Luxembourg 1.1
Netherlands 2.2
Austria 3.0
Portugal 3.0
Finland 1.9
Sweden 2.9
Britain 3.0
